Communication overhead against the stdlib `concurrent.futures` pools (Apple
M4 Pro, from `benchmarks/mizu-stdlib-bench.py`).

Against `ProcessPoolExecutor` (tasks run in separate processes, with pickled
payloads):

| Benchmark | pymizu | ProcessPoolExecutor | Speedup |
|----|----|----|----|
| Trivial task round trip | 0.7 µs | 94.2 µs | 135x |
| Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 18,500 tasks/s | 129x |
| Parallel map overhead, trivial function, 4 workers | 0.4 µs/elt* | 70.3 µs/elt | 176x |
| Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 4.3 ms | 129 ms | 30x |

Against `ThreadPoolExecutor` (tasks share one process, so the GIL caps
CPU-bound work at a single core):

| Benchmark | pymizu | ThreadPoolExecutor | Speedup |
|----|----|----|----|
| Trivial task round trip | 0.7 µs | 9.5 µs | 14x |
| Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 405,000 tasks/s | 5.9x |
| Parallel map overhead, trivial function, 4 workers | 0.4 µs/elt* | 2.6 µs/elt | 6.5x |
| Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 4.3 ms | 50 ms | 12x |

Against `InterpreterPoolExecutor` (Python 3.14+, subinterpreters with
per-interpreter GILs): on the trivial-task rows it lands between the
thread and process pools — 21.3 µs per round trip and 59,600 tasks/s
pipelined on this machine (measured 2026-10-07).
The map rows it cannot run at all: task payloads must be shareable —
builtin scalars, plain containers, or buffer-protocol objects — so
numpy arrays and numpy scalars raise `NotShareableError`.

\* elt = element; microseconds of wall time per map element.

These rows measure communication overhead — the cost pymizu is built to
remove.
The stdlib pools remain the general solution: they run anywhere Python runs,
with no platform requirements.

## How pymizu compares

pymizu occupies a specific point in the design space: parallelism across
processes on a single machine, with data moving through shared memory
instead of serialized copies.
The tools below overlap at the edges; the differences are in what has to
run, how data moves, and what survives a crash.

| Tool | What runs | How data moves | Best for |
|----|----|----|----|
| `multiprocessing` / `concurrent.futures` | Nothing beyond the stdlib | Pickle copies per task | Coarse tasks, maximum portability |
| `joblib` | A reusable worker pool (loky) | Pickle; large arrays memmapped to a temp folder | Coarse parallel loops, anywhere Python runs |
| `ipyparallel` | A controller process plus engines | Pickle over ZeroMQ sockets | Interactive parallelism from Jupyter |
| Ray | A runtime: scheduler, object store, dashboard | Object store (zero-copy reads on one node) | Cluster scaling, actors, GPU placement |
| Dask | A scheduler (plus workers for `distributed`) | Copies between processes; shared heap only on the threaded scheduler | Out-of-core dataframes and arrays |
| Free-threaded CPython | Nothing; threads | Nothing; threads share one heap | Single-language CPU work needing no isolation |
| `concurrent.interpreters` | Nothing beyond the stdlib | Shareable types only: builtins copy, buffers share; numpy rejected | Isolated parallelism without processes (3.14+) |
| ZeroMQ | Nothing; a library | Socket copies | General messaging patterns |
| pymizu | Nothing; a library | Shared-memory views, µs handoff | Fine-grained tasks, large arrays, R interop |

### Process pools: `multiprocessing`, `concurrent.futures`, joblib, ipyparallel

The stdlib pools are the baseline the tables above measure.
joblib's `Parallel`/`delayed` is the long-standing answer for an
embarrassingly parallel loop over numpy data, and its `loky` backend is
the closest in spirit to pymizu: a reusable process pool that memmaps
arrays past a size threshold to a temp folder instead of pickling them.
That removes the pickle copy, but the array still round-trips through the
filesystem and a task round trip stays in the millisecond range.
ipyparallel answers the same question for Jupyter: a controller process
brokers pickled messages over ZeroMQ sockets to engine processes — a
controller in the loop and socket copies are the price of its generality.
`multiprocessing.shared_memory` exposes raw shared buffers and leaves
synchronization, lifetime tracking, and crash cleanup to you; pymizu is
that idea finished — the same pages, with the waiting, framing, and
peer-death detection built in.

### Distributed frameworks: Ray and Dask

Ray and Dask answer a bigger question — spreading work across machines —
and pay for it on one machine: a local Ray instance still starts a
scheduler, object store, and dashboard, and a task round trip costs on
the order of a millisecond; Dask's `distributed` scheduler is similar,
while its process-free threaded scheduler shares memory but is capped by
the GIL for Python-level work.
Ray's object store does read numpy arrays without copying on the same
node, so the honest difference is not capability but overhead and
footprint: for a cluster, actors, or out-of-core dataframes, use them;
when the work fits one machine and the tasks are measured in
microseconds, the framework overhead dominates the work.

### Modern CPython: free-threading and subinterpreters

Python 3.14 officially supports a build with the GIL removed, in which
threads share one heap and exchange data with no copies at all.
That is the right answer for single-language CPU parallelism when
isolation is not needed: a crashing thread takes the process down, C
extensions must be built and validated for it, and it does nothing for
crossing into R.
pymizu targets the standard GIL build and does not yet support the
free-threaded one; the two approaches solve different problems — threads
trade isolation for sharing, pymizu keeps the isolation and makes the
sharing cheap.

Python 3.14 also added `concurrent.interpreters` to the stdlib
([PEP 734](https://peps.python.org/pep-0734/)): multiple interpreters in
one process, each with its own GIL, so CPU work parallelizes without new
processes on the standard build.
Objects passed between interpreters must be shareable: builtin scalars
and plain containers of them cross as copies, buffer-protocol objects
can share their underlying memory (synchronization left to you), and
anything else — numpy arrays included — is rejected outright.
The isolation is real but not OS-level — a fatal error in one interpreter
ends the process — and the surrounding machinery (queues, lifetimes,
crash handling) is yours to build.
It is also 3.14 and later only; pymizu runs on 3.10 and later.

### Messaging: ZeroMQ

ZeroMQ is the canonical answer for moving bytes between processes, and
pymizu's channels play in the same space — but the bytes move over
sockets, so every message is copied, and the distribution patterns are
yours to design: it is a building block (ipyparallel is built on it),
not a task pool.
A pymizu channel plays the same role with the copies removed — written
once, read in place.

### The one thing only pymizu does

A pool whose workers are R processes, exchanging numpy arrays and data
frames as shared-memory views ([R interop](interop.qmd)).
None of the tools above cross the language boundary.

The short version: choose pymizu when the work fits one machine, when
tasks are fine-grained or arrays large, or when R needs to be in the
loop; choose Ray or Dask when you outgrow one machine or need their
collections, `concurrent.interpreters` when you want stdlib-only
isolation and can require Python 3.14, and free-threading when one
language and shared-everything is acceptable.

`benchmarks/mizu-bench.py` runs the pymizu rows standalone,
`benchmarks/mizu-stdlib-bench.py` the comparison, and
`benchmarks/crosslang-map-bench.py` the cross-language map comparison.
The scripts are report-only and assert nothing about the numbers (CI runner
timing is too variable); dated records live in `benchmarks/notes.md`.
